title: Group Axioms, Uniqueness and the Reversal Rule
quickIdea: A group is an associative operation with an identity and an inverse for every element. The identity and each inverse are unique, and inverses reverse the order of a product.
remember: Group axioms: closure, associativity, a two-sided identity e, and for each a an element a^-1 with a a^-1 = a^-1 a = e. Commutativity is not required.
The identity is unique: if e and e' are both identities then e = e e' = e'. Each inverse is unique: if b and c both invert a then b = b e = b (a c) = (b a) c = c.
(a b)^-1 = b^-1 a^-1: the order reverses. It collapses to a^-1 b^-1 only in an abelian group, which is why the mistake survives every abelian example.
Cancellation holds in every group: a b = a c implies b = c, by multiplying on the left by a^-1. This one move is the whole proof of the 2022 commutativity question.
The equation a x = b has exactly one solution, x = a^-1 b; the equation x a = b has exactly one, x = b a^-1. In a non-abelian group the two answers differ.
A group in which every element is its own inverse is abelian: a b = (a b)^-1 = b^-1 a^-1 = b a.
Finite shortcut: for a finite set with an associative operation, the two cancellation laws already force a group, so no separate inverse check is needed.

example.prompt: In S3, the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} under composition, verify (a b)^-1 = b^-1 a^-1 for a = (1 2) and b = (1 2 3).
example.work: Composition is read right to left. a b applies b then a: 1 goes to 2 then to 1, 2 goes to 3 then stays at 3, 3 goes to 1 then to 2, so a b = (2 3), whose inverse is itself. On the other side b^-1 = (1 3 2) and a^-1 = (1 2), so b^-1 a^-1 applies (1 2) first: 1 goes to 2 then to 1, 2 goes to 1 then to 3, 3 goes to 3 then to 2, giving (2 3) again.
example.answer: Both sides equal (2 3), which is its own inverse; the reversal b^-1 a^-1 is exactly what reproduces (a b)^-1.

gateAngle: GATE rarely asks for the axioms; it asks whether a structure is a group, or which manipulation is legal. When a question multiplies on both sides, the legal moves are left and right multiplication by an inverse, cancellation, and the reversal rule for products.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: In a group, if a b = e, what is b?
variations.answer: b = a^-1, by multiplying a b = e on the left by a^-1.
variations.why: The inverse is unique, so exhibiting one element that works identifies it; this is the shortest possible proof of an inverse claim.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: In a group, solve a x b = c for x.
variations.why: Multiply by a^-1 on the left and by b^-1 on the right. The x is trapped between two elements, which is exactly why the order matters in a non-abelian group.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A finite set S carries an associative operation in which both cancellation laws hold. Must it be a group?
variations.answer: Yes. In a finite table, cancellation makes every row and column a permutation of S, so an identity appears and every element has an inverse.
variations.why: This is the finite shortcut GATE can exploit; for infinite sets it fails, since (N, +) cancels and is not a group.

trap.why: Inverses reverse order. The swap is invisible in every abelian example, so the error survives practice and then breaks the first time a permutation group appears.

check.question: In a group, simplify (a b c)^-1.
check.explanation: Apply the reversal rule twice: (a (b c))^-1 = (b c)^-1 a^-1 = c^-1 b^-1 a^-1. Each factor keeps its own inverse and the order of the factors is reversed, which is the statement to remember.
